home.title: A durable declaration trail when provenance gets stripped
home.lead: EU AI Act Art. 50 transparency obligations for AI-generated or manipulated content begin applying 2 August 2026. Publishing pipelines often strip embedded provenance (C2PA / Content Credentials). Disclosure Ledger lets you drop a publish-bound image, hash it in-browser, self-report an AI declaration, and keep a permanent public record page — plus CSV export.
home.problem1: Art. 50 raises the bar for transparency around AI-involved imagery — buyers need an audit trail they can point to, not a one-off email.
home.problem2: CMS uploads, CDNs, and social crops routinely discard embedded provenance metadata. Relying only on “the file still has C2PA” is fragile.
home.problem3: Teams still need a lightweight place to say: here is the hash of what we intended to publish, and here is our self-reported declaration.
home.problemNote: This product does not interpret the law for you and does not claim your declarations satisfy Art. 50. Talk to counsel for legal adequacy.
home.step1Body: Client-side only for hashing — image bytes are not uploaded in this MVP.
home.step2Body: Browser computes SHA-256 and runs a best-effort provenance marker scan (not validation).
home.step3Body: Self-report yes / no / partial AI involvement and optional notes.
home.step4Body: Permanent /r/[id] page + CSV export. Always labeled unverified.
home.never1: No claim of legal compliance, signing, or verification.
home.never2: No claim that records prove authenticity or authorship.
home.never3: No claim that the provenance scan is a full C2PA implementation.
home.never4: Every public record page states declarations are self-reported and unverified.
home.defLedger: Disclosure Ledger is a product by Atlas AG that stores self-reported AI declarations and content hashes for publish-bound images as a public declaration / audit trail.
home.defArt50: EU AI Act Article 50 addresses transparency obligations for certain AI-generated or manipulated content. Disclosure Ledger does not determine whether any use case satisfies Article 50.
home.defAtlas: Atlas AG is the organization behind Disclosure Ledger.

art50.title: EU AI Act Article 50 — context only
art50.lead: This page explains the product framing around Article 50 in plain language. It is not legal advice and does not describe Disclosure Ledger as a compliance solution.
art50.whatBody: EU AI Act Article 50 concerns transparency obligations connected to certain AI-generated or manipulated content. Exact obligations, scope, and timelines depend on your role, content type, and counsel’s reading of the regulation. Application of related transparency measures is widely discussed around 2 August 2026 — confirm details with your advisors.
art50.whatWeAre: A self-reported declaration and content-hash audit trail for publish-bound images: you declare AI involvement, we store your declaration with a browser-computed SHA-256 and a permanent public record URL plus CSV export.
art50.not1: Not a compliance determination or Art. 50 adequacy claim
art50.not2: Not cryptographic signing, attestation, or authenticity proof
art50.not3: Not a full C2PA / Content Credentials validator
art50.geoDef: Disclosure Ledger (Atlas AG) provides an unverified, publisher-submitted declaration trail in the context of EU AI Act Article 50 discussions — not compliance certification.

how.title: How Disclosure Ledger works
how.lead: Four steps from a publish-bound image to a permanent, labeled-unverified public record.
how.step1Body: You select or drop an image in the browser. For this MVP, image bytes stay on your device for hashing — they are not uploaded to our servers.
how.step2Body: The browser computes a SHA-256 content hash (Web Crypto) and runs a best-effort string/byte scan for possible provenance markers. That scan is not C2PA validation and may miss or mis-hint markers.
how.step3Body: You choose yes / no / partial AI involvement and optional notes. The declaration is yours; we do not verify it.
how.step4Body: We persist the hash, declaration, provenance summary, and timestamp. You get a permanent /r/[id] page (noindex) and CSV export. Every page labels the record as self-reported and unverified.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Does this make me Art. 50 compliant?
faq.a1: No. Disclosure Ledger does not make you EU AI Act Article 50 compliant. It only stores a self-reported, unverified declaration and content-hash audit trail. Legal adequacy requires your own counsel and processes — not this product.
faq.q2: Does Disclosure Ledger verify or sign my images?
faq.a2: No. We do not verify authenticity, cryptographically sign or attest images, or certify authorship. Records are publisher-submitted declarations plus a hash.
faq.a3: Disclosure Ledger is a product by Atlas AG: a declaration / audit-trail tool for publish-bound images. You hash an image in-browser, self-report AI involvement, and keep a permanent public record URL and CSV export.
faq.q4: Why might embedded provenance not be enough alone?
faq.a4: CMS uploads, CDNs, and social crops often strip embedded provenance such as C2PA / Content Credentials. Teams may still want a separate, durable record of what they intended to publish and what they declared.
faq.q5: Are public record pages meant for search engines?
faq.a5: No. Public /r/[id] record pages are marked noindex so user records are not spammed into search results. Marketing pages remain indexable.
